prompt: How does the central single bond of 1,3-butadiene (between carbons 2 and 3) compare with the bond between carbons 2 and 3 of butane?

choices.text: It is shorter: 147 pm versus 153 pm
It is longer: 153 pm versus 147 pm
choices.why: The numbers are the other way round. The central bond of 1,3-butadiene is 147 pm, about 6 pm shorter than butane's 153 pm.

choices.text: It is the same length, 153 pm, since both are single bonds
choices.why: Both are single bonds, but the one in 1,3-butadiene is shorter than expected: 147 pm.

choices.text: It is longer, because sp2 orbitals have less s character than sp3 orbitals
choices.why: sp2 orbitals have more s character (33%) than sp3 orbitals (25%), which makes the bond shorter, not longer.

explanation: One property that sets conjugated dienes apart from nonconjugated ones is that the central single bond is shorter than expected. In 1,3-butadiene it is 147 pm long, some 6 pm shorter than the 153 pm bond between carbons 2 and 3 of butane.

prompt: When two p atomic orbitals combine to form a π bond, what molecular orbitals result?

choices.text: One lower-energy bonding MO and one higher-energy antibonding MO with a node between the nuclei
Two bonding MOs, both lower in energy than the starting p orbitals
choices.why: Two atomic orbitals give one bonding and one antibonding MO. Only the bonding one is lower in energy than the p orbitals.

choices.text: One bonding MO with a node between the nuclei and one antibonding MO with no node
choices.why: It's the reverse. The antibonding orbital (ψ_2*) has the node between the nuclei; the bonding orbital (ψ_1) has none.

choices.text: A single bonding MO, which holds both π electrons
choices.why: Combining two atomic orbitals always gives two molecular orbitals: one bonding and one antibonding.

explanation: Two p orbitals combine to give two π MOs. The bonding MO (ψ_1) is lower in energy than the starting p orbitals; the antibonding MO (ψ_2*) is higher in energy and has a node between the nuclei. Both π electrons occupy the bonding orbital, so energy is lowered and a stable bond forms (Figure 14.1.1).

prompt: A monosubstituted alkene such as 1-butene has ΔH°_hydrog of about −126 kJ/mol. What ΔH°_hydrog, including its sign, would you expect for a diene whose two monosubstituted double bonds don't interact, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Two independent double bonds should each release about 126 kJ/mol: 2 × (−126 kJ/mol) = −252 kJ/mol. The nonconjugated diene 1,4-pentadiene (−253 kJ/mol) meets this expectation, but the conjugated diene 1,3-butadiene (−236 kJ/mol) does not.

prompt: Two monosubstituted double bonds should give ΔH°_hydrog ≈ −252 kJ/mol, but the measured value for 1,3-butadiene is −236 kJ/mol. By about how many kJ/mol is 1,3-butadiene more stable than expected?
explanation: −236 kJ/mol − (−252 kJ/mol) = 16 kJ/mol. 1,3-Butadiene releases about 16 kJ/mol (3.8 kcal/mol) less heat than expected because it contains less energy to start with: the conjugated diene is about 16 kJ/mol more stable than expected.

prompt: Which diene would you expect to have ΔH°_hydrog close to −252 kJ/mol, about twice the value for a monosubstituted alkene?

choices.text: 1,5-Hexadiene, H2C=CHCH2CH2CH=CH2
1,3-Butadiene, H2C=CHCH=CH2
choices.why: 1,3-Butadiene is conjugated. Its ΔH°_hydrog is only −236 kJ/mol, because conjugation makes it about 16 kJ/mol more stable than expected.

choices.text: 2-Methyl-1,3-butadiene (isoprene)
choices.why: Isoprene is a conjugated diene. Its ΔH°_hydrog is −229 kJ/mol (Table 14.1.1), well short of −252 kJ/mol.

choices.text: Allene, H2C=C=CH2
choices.why: Allene's adjacent double bonds give ΔH°_hydrog = −298 kJ/mol, much more negative than −252 kJ/mol.

explanation: In 1,5-hexadiene the two monosubstituted double bonds are separated by two CH2 groups, so they are not conjugated and don't interact. Nonconjugated dienes such as 1,4-pentadiene (−253 kJ/mol) have ΔH°_hydrog close to twice the −126 kJ/mol of a monosubstituted alkene.

prompt: 1-Butene (monosubstituted) has ΔH°_hydrog = −126 kJ/mol and 2-methylpropene (disubstituted) has ΔH°_hydrog = −119 kJ/mol. By how many kJ/mol is the disubstituted alkene's value less negative?
explanation: −119 kJ/mol − (−126 kJ/mol) = 7 kJ/mol. The more highly substituted alkene releases less heat on hydrogenation because it contains less energy to start with, so it is more stable. The section draws the same kind of conclusion for conjugated dienes.

prompt: Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) has one disubstituted double bond (about −119 kJ/mol expected) and one monosubstituted double bond (about −126 kJ/mol expected). Its measured ΔH°_hydrog is −229 kJ/mol. By how many kJ/mol is isoprene more stable than two isolated double bonds would predict?
explanation: Expected: −119 kJ/mol + (−126 kJ/mol) = −245 kJ/mol. Measured: −229 kJ/mol (Table 14.1.1). −229 − (−245) = 16 kJ/mol, about the same extra stability that conjugation gives 1,3-butadiene.

prompt: Why does a more stable alkene or diene release less heat when it is hydrogenated?

choices.text: It contains less energy to start with
It contains more energy to start with
choices.why: A compound with more energy would release more heat, not less. The more stable compound starts lower in energy.

choices.text: It takes up less hydrogen
choices.why: Each double bond takes up one H2 however stable it is; 1,3-butadiene and 1,4-pentadiene both add two. The difference lies in the starting energy.

choices.text: It reacts more slowly with hydrogen
choices.why: ΔH°_hydrog measures the heat released, not the rate. Less heat is released because the compound starts lower in energy.

explanation: More highly substituted alkenes and conjugated dienes release less heat on hydrogenation because they contain less energy to start with. A less negative ΔH°_hydrog therefore signals a more stable compound.

prompt: Allene, H2C=C=CH2, has ΔH°_hydrog = −298 kJ/mol, while −252 kJ/mol is expected for two isolated monosubstituted double bonds. By how many kJ/mol is allene's value more negative than expected?
explanation: −298 kJ/mol − (−252 kJ/mol) = −46 kJ/mol. Allene releases 46 kJ/mol more heat than expected, so it contains more energy and is less stable than a nonconjugated diene (Exercise 14.1.1).

prompt: Based on heats of hydrogenation, how do a conjugated diene, a nonconjugated diene and an allene rank in stability, from most to least stable?

choices.text: Conjugated diene > nonconjugated diene > allene
Allene > conjugated diene > nonconjugated diene
choices.why: Allene has the most negative ΔH°_hydrog (−298 kJ/mol), so it is the least stable, not the most.

choices.text: Nonconjugated diene > conjugated diene > allene
choices.why: The conjugated diene releases less heat (−236 kJ/mol for 1,3-butadiene) than a nonconjugated diene (−253 kJ/mol for 1,4-pentadiene), so it is more stable.

choices.text: Conjugated diene > allene > nonconjugated diene
choices.why: Allene releases even more heat than a nonconjugated diene (−298 versus about −252 kJ/mol), so it is the least stable of the three.

explanation: The less heat released, the more stable the compound. 1,3-Butadiene (−236 kJ/mol) is more stable than the −252 kJ/mol expected, 1,4-pentadiene (−253 kJ/mol) is about as expected, and allene (−298 kJ/mol) is less stable than expected (Exercise 14.1.1).

prompt: According to valence bond theory, why is the central single bond of a conjugated diene shorter and stronger than a typical alkane C–C bond?

choices.text: It forms from σ overlap of sp2 orbitals, which have more s character than sp3 orbitals
It forms from σ overlap of sp3 orbitals, which have more s character than sp2 orbitals
choices.why: sp3 orbitals have less s character (25%) than sp2 orbitals (33%). Alkane C–C bonds use sp3 orbitals; the diene's central bond uses sp2.

choices.text: It forms from sideways overlap of p orbitals, making it a π bond
choices.why: The central bond is a σ bond. Its extra strength comes from the hybrid orbitals that form it.

choices.text: It forms from σ overlap of sp orbitals, which have the most s character
choices.why: The carbons of a conjugated diene are sp2-hybridized, not sp.

explanation: Typical C–C single bonds come from σ overlap of sp3 orbitals (25% s), but the central bond of a conjugated diene comes from σ overlap of sp2 orbitals (33% s). Electrons in orbitals with more s character are closer to the nucleus, so the bond is somewhat shorter and stronger.

prompt: How many π molecular orbitals result when the four adjacent p atomic orbitals of a conjugated diene combine?
explanation: Combining four p atomic orbitals gives four π MOs: two bonding (ψ_1 and ψ_2) and two antibonding (ψ_3* and ψ_4*) (Figure 14.1.2).

prompt: In the ground state of 1,3-butadiene, which π molecular orbitals hold the four π electrons?

choices.text: ψ_1 and ψ_2, the two bonding orbitals
ψ_1 only
choices.why: Each orbital holds two electrons, so four π electrons fill both bonding orbitals, ψ_1 and ψ_2.

choices.text: One electron in each of ψ_1, ψ_2, ψ_3* and ψ_4*
choices.why: Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first, two per orbital, so the antibonding orbitals stay empty.

choices.text: ψ_3* and ψ_4*, the two antibonding orbitals
choices.why: The antibonding orbitals are higher in energy and are left vacant in the ground state.

explanation: The four π electrons occupy the two bonding orbitals, ψ_1 and ψ_2, leaving the antibonding orbitals ψ_3* and ψ_4* vacant.

prompt: How many nodes between nuclei does the ψ_3* molecular orbital of 1,3-butadiene have?
explanation: ψ_1 has no nodes between nuclei, ψ_2 has one, ψ_3* has two and ψ_4*, the highest-energy MO, has three. The number of nodes increases with the energy of the orbital.

prompt: How does the number of nodes between nuclei change across the π molecular orbitals of 1,3-butadiene?

choices.text: It increases as the energy of the orbital increases
It decreases as the energy of the orbital increases
choices.why: It's the reverse: the lowest-energy orbital, ψ_1, has no nodes and the highest, ψ_4*, has three.

choices.text: Every π orbital has exactly one node
choices.why: The count varies: ψ_1 has none, ψ_2 one, ψ_3* two and ψ_4* three.

choices.text: Only the antibonding orbitals have nodes
choices.why: The bonding orbital ψ_2 also has one node between nuclei.

explanation: The number of nodes between nuclei increases as the energy level of the orbital increases: 0 for ψ_1, 1 for ψ_2, 2 for ψ_3* and 3 for ψ_4* (Figure 14.1.2).

prompt: Which description fits the ψ_2 molecular orbital of 1,3-butadiene?

choices.text: Bonding, with one node between nuclei
Antibonding, with one node between nuclei
choices.why: ψ_2 is the second bonding orbital. The antibonding orbitals are ψ_3* and ψ_4*.

choices.text: Bonding, with no nodes between nuclei
choices.why: That describes ψ_1, the lowest-energy π MO.

choices.text: Antibonding, with two nodes between nuclei
choices.why: That describes ψ_3*, the lower of the two antibonding orbitals.

explanation: ψ_2, the π MO of next-lowest energy after ψ_1, has one node between nuclei and is bonding. Above it lie the antibonding orbitals ψ_3* (two nodes) and ψ_4* (three nodes).

prompt: According to molecular orbital theory, why is 1,3-butadiene more stable than the nonconjugated 1,4-pentadiene?

choices.text: In ψ_1, carbons 2 and 3 have a bonding interaction, giving the central bond partial double-bond character
Its π electrons stay localized in two separate double bonds, keeping them far apart
choices.why: It's the opposite: in a conjugated diene the π electrons are delocalized over the whole π framework.

choices.text: It has more π electrons than 1,4-pentadiene, making its π bonds stronger
choices.why: Both dienes have two double bonds and four π electrons. The difference is how their p orbitals interact.

choices.text: Two of its π electrons sit in antibonding orbitals, which lowers the energy
choices.why: All four π electrons are in the bonding MOs ψ_1 and ψ_2. Electrons in antibonding orbitals would raise the energy.

explanation: In a conjugated diene, the lowest-energy π MO (ψ_1) has a favorable bonding interaction between carbons 2 and 3 that is absent in a nonconjugated diene. That gives the central single bond some double-bond character, making it stronger and shorter than a typical single bond.

prompt: Why does delocalizing the π electrons over the whole π framework lower the energy of 1,3-butadiene?

choices.text: The bonding electrons can be closer to more nuclei
The bonding electrons are kept farther from all the nuclei
choices.why: Delocalization brings the electrons closer to more nuclei, not farther away.

choices.text: The π electrons move into the antibonding orbitals
choices.why: The π electrons stay in the bonding MOs ψ_1 and ψ_2; the antibonding orbitals are empty.

choices.text: Two of the π electrons are lost from the molecule
choices.why: No electrons are lost. The same four π electrons are spread over all four carbons.

explanation: In 1,3-butadiene the π electrons are delocalized over the entire π framework rather than localized between two specific nuclei. Delocalization lets the bonding electrons be closer to more nuclei, which means lower energy and greater stability.

prompt: How has isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) been prepared industrially?

choices.text: By acid-catalyzed double dehydration of 3-methyl-1,3-butanediol
By acid-catalyzed single dehydration of 3-methyl-1,3-butanediol
choices.why: Losing one water would leave one OH group and only one double bond. Two waters must be lost to form isoprene's two double bonds.

choices.text: By base-induced elimination of HBr from 3-bromocyclohexene
choices.why: That reaction gives 1,3-cyclohexadiene, the section's other diene-preparation example.

choices.text: By hydrogenation of 3-methyl-1,3-butanediol
choices.why: Hydrogenation adds H2. Isoprene forms when the diol loses two molecules of water.

explanation: Isoprene has been prepared industrially by the acid-catalyzed double dehydration of 3-methyl-1,3-butanediol: heating with aluminum oxide removes two molecules of water, creating the two conjugated double bonds.

prompt: How is 1,3-cyclohexadiene made from cyclohexene in the section's example?

choices.text: Allylic bromination with NBS gives 3-bromocyclohexene; potassium tert-butoxide then eliminates HBr
HBr addition gives bromocyclohexane; potassium tert-butoxide then eliminates HBr
choices.why: Eliminating HBr from bromocyclohexane just gives cyclohexene back. An allylic halide is needed so that elimination creates a second, conjugated double bond.

choices.text: Allylic bromination with NBS gives 3-bromocyclohexene; H2 then hydrogenates it
choices.why: Hydrogenation would remove a double bond. The second double bond comes from base-induced elimination of HBr.

choices.text: Potassium tert-butoxide alone removes H2 from cyclohexene
choices.why: Cyclohexene has no leaving group to eliminate. NBS first puts a bromine in the allylic position.

explanation: Conjugated dienes can be made by base-induced elimination of HX from an allylic halide. Cyclohexene reacts with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) in light to give 3-bromocyclohexene, and potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butyl alcohol then eliminates HBr to give 1,3-cyclohexadiene (76%).
